content: Your doctor has prescribed oxacillin, an antibiotic, to treat your infection. This medication can be administered either by injection into a large muscle, such as the buttock or hip, or through an intravenous (IV) infusion. If given intravenously, the drug will be added to a fluid that drips into your vein via a needle or catheter over approximately 30 minutes, and this process will be repeated four to six times daily. Oxacillin works by eliminating bacteria responsible for infections, including pneumonia, meningitis, and infections of the urinary tract, skin, bones, joints, blood, and heart valves. In some cases, oxacillin may be prescribed for other conditions; consult your doctor or pharmacist for further details. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and any potential side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how well your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting oxacillin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to oxacillin, penicillin, cephalosporins, or any other medications. Additionally, provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are currently taking, including antibiotics and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of asthma, hay fever, or any kidney, liver, or gastrointestinal conditions, particularly colitis. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. Should you become pregnant while taking oxacillin, contact your doctor immediately. If you have diabetes and routinely check your urine for sugar, use Clinistix or TesTape for testing, as oxacillin may cause false-positive results with Clinitest tablets. Before administering oxacillin, inspect the solution carefully. It should appear clear and free of any floating particles. Check the bag or container for leaks by gently squeezing it or observing it closely. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Instead, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your healthcare provider's instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not discontinue the treatment on your own, as this could worsen your infection and potentially lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you encounter a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may advise you to stop the infusion. Oxacillin may cause side effects. Minor side effects include upset stomach and diarrhea. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your healthcare provider. Serious side effects require immediate medical attention and include rash, itching, fever, chills, facial swelling, wheezing, difficulty breathing, unusual bleeding or bruising, dizziness, seizures, or a sore mouth or throat. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor can report it to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. If you are receiving oxacillin intravenously, your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several days' worth of medication at a time. Store the medication in the refrigerator or freezer as instructed. Before using your next dose, remove it from the refrigerator one hour in advance and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to reach room temperature. If you are storing additional oxacillin in the freezer, transfer a 24-hour supply to the refrigerator each day. Do not refreeze the medication. If you are receiving oxacillin intramuscularly, follow your healthcare provider's storage instructions carefully. Always store your medication and supplies in a clean, dry place, and keep them out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will also instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving oxacillin intravenously or subcutaneously, be aware of the signs of a catheter-related infection, which can occur at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin. Symptoms include tenderness, warmth, irritation, drainage, redness, swelling, and pain. If you notice any of these symptoms, inform your healthcare provider immediately. Oxacillin is also marketed under the brand name Bactocill®.
